newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria says opposition, foreigners behind bombs.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says opposition, foreigners behind bombs.

text.p: Nigeria's police chief Ibrahim Coomasie said on Thursday that investigations had shown the opposition NADECO group and foreign nations were behind a spate of recent bomb attacks in Lagos.

Inspector-General Coomasie told a news conference in the capital Abuja that a former army chief, retired Lieutenant-General Alani Akinrinade now exiled in London and who is a member of NADECO was implicated in investigations.
"NADECO and their chieftains both within and outside Nigeria have been the brains behind these bombings. Security agencies are also investigating the involvement of some foreign countries," he said.
NADECO has denied any involvement in the bombs.
On Wednesday the military authorities disclosed that 22 people had been arrested in connection with the bombs but did not identify them.
Lagos, centre of opposition to military rule in Nigeria, has been rocked by three bomb attacks on military targets since December which have killed three soldiers and wounded scores.
Coomasie also linked former finance minister and NADECO member Olu Falae with the bombings. Falae was arrested two weeks ago but police did not say why.
His family said the arrest was in connection with the bombings but denied that he was in any way involved.
But Coomasie said investigations had shown an agent of the opposition identified as Nelson Gbolahan Kassim, whom the police said was killed in a bungled bomb blast last November, had met with Falae.
"Chief Falae also contributed the sum of 40,000 naira ($500) for RF which is decoded as radio frequency," he said.
Africa's most populous nation has been in crisis since 1993 when the army scrapped a presidential vote aimed at restoring democracy.
Moshood Abiola, the businessman presumed to have won the annulled poll has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the military government.
NADECO, an umbrellla organisation of human rights and pro-democracy groups came into existence in 1994 and was behind Abiola's declaration of himself as president.
Coomasie gave a detailed account of how previous bomb attacks since January last year were planned from Akinrinade's house in Lagos.
He also provided Akinrinade's London home address, where he said a Nigerian businessman identified as Dr Amos Arogundade, who had been declared wanted over the bomb attacks was staying.
